vignette: He sits across from me, hands folded tightly over his knees. He is of Southeast Asian descent, though he speaks of the valley that holds his earliest trauma with the same measured distance he keeps from his own memories. At eighty, his posture remains straight, the way a man who learned to stand alert in a collapsing world still stands now. He speaks in even tones, but his eyes track the hallway behind me whenever a floorboard creaks. We have met seven times, and the story he offers moves forward like a river finding its bed, returning again and again to a place where the sky used to tear open without warning. He arrives at twenty-four as a relief worker. The maps in his pack are outdated, the radio batteries are dying, the air hangs thick with dust and diesel. He remembers the rhythm of mortar fire like a metronome, and how he learns to calculate distance not by sight but by the pause between flash and sound. One afternoon, the triage tent collapses. He pulls three people free before the canvas gives way entirely. He holds his own hands now, turning them over slowly, as if checking for dust that never washes out. He describes the quiet afterward more vividly than the noise-the way the survivors stop speaking, the way he keeps waiting for the next ground tremor even though the earth has gone still. Life moves forward, though he moves slower. He marries, raises a daughter, and eventually leaves humanitarian work behind. His wife passes five years ago, quietly, in her sleep. He says he likes that she does not wake startled. Now he lives alone in a high-rise overlooking a city that never stops humming. He works as a data scientist, consulting on predictive models for municipal infrastructure. He tells me how much he enjoys the clarity of a clean dataset, how rows and columns feel like a world that finally behaves. Yet when his screen floods with anomalous readings-sudden spikes, corrupted files-he stops typing. His breathing shallows. He closes his laptop, walks to the window, and watches the traffic merge like a slow-moving river. He calls it noise, but his shoulders stay hunched, his jaw tight, as if waiting for the other shoe to drop. Sleep remains the hardest terrain. He sets three alarms, checks the deadbolt twice, and keeps the television on low until dawn. When he does drift off, he wakes with a start, heart hammering, convinced he hears the same metallic shriek that used to precede artillery. He tells me he no longer watches the news, not out of indifference, but because the cadence of emergency broadcasts triggers a physical recoil. He avoids supermarkets during peak hours. He says it feels easier to order everything online, to receive cardboard boxes on the same day each week, to control the variables. He has built a life around predictability, yet his mind keeps returning to the uncountable variables of that valley: the sandbags that shift, the radio static, the face of a boy who does not wake. In our most recent session, he traces the rim of his teacup with his thumb, speaking of how he once thought healing means forgetting the weight. Now he knows it is simply learning how to carry it without dropping everything else. He looks out the window as a low thunder rolls across the afternoon. He does not flinch, but his pen stills. He breathes in, slowly, and writes a single line in his notebook before folding it shut.
